722.title: the birth of the cousins
722.hook: a forest sage with blazing eyes comes to a palace bedroom, a frightened widow shuts her eyes, and a son is born blind
722.carry: a widow too frightened to look
722.howItsDone: The ancient custom in this story, called niyoga, is described in old texts and the epics; it is not practiced in Hindu families today, and the story is told for what it shows about the Kuru line.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Satyavati thinking of her firstborn, and Vyasa appearing at once. She thinks of him; he comes.

Vyasa comes to the palace straight from the forest, and he looks it. The text describes him: dark skin, matted hair the color of copper, a rough beard, blazing eyes, and a smell no one would call perfume. His mother has asked him to give the house of the Kurus a son. He agrees, and asks that they wait first. Satyavati answers: there is no time.
screen: `A SAGE FROM THE FOREST.` → `HE ASKS FOR TIME.` → `THERE IS NO TIME.`

segments.voice: This begins a new part: the birth of the cousins. First the fathers are born, then the cousins who will one day face each other across a battlefield. It starts with an ancient custom: when a man died without children, a learned man could be invited to father them in his name, so the line would go on. Vyasa says the widows should first keep a vow, to be ready. Satyavati says the kingdom can't wait for a king. So Vyasa says: then let the princess bear my looks, my smell, my grim face. That will be her vow. Satyavati tells the elder widow, Ambika, that a brother-in-law will come to her tonight. Ambika thinks of the heroes of the Kuru house, and waits. The lamp is lit, and in comes Vyasa, with his blazing eyes and copper hair. She's afraid, and she shuts her eyes, and keeps them shut. Afterward Vyasa tells his mother: the son will be strong and wise, a fine prince. But because his mother closed her eyes, he will be born blind. Satyavati answers at once: a blind man can't be king of the Kurus. Give the family another. That son is Dhritarashtra. Vyasa ties the blindness to Ambika's closed eyes, but the text doesn't make her a villain. It shows a widow too frightened to look, a mother in a hurry, and a son who will spend his life near a throne he can't fully have.
screen: `AN OLD CUSTOM FOR A LINE.` · `NO TIME TO WAIT.` · `AMBIKA SHUTS HER EYES.` · `DHRITARASHTRA, BORN BLIND.`

segments.voice: Ambika closed her eyes because she was afraid. Bring to mind something you've been not looking at, a bill, a conversation, a feeling, and without opening it, turn toward it a little, the way you'd turn toward a sound in the next room. Notice the fear, if it's there, and breathe beside it.
Dhritarashtra, born blind because his mother, Ambika, couldn't bear to look at the sage who fathered him.
Your line: a widow too frightened to look. One night's fear shaped a whole life. See you tomorrow.

723.title: the birth of the cousins
723.hook: the younger widow turns pale, the elder sends her maid in her place, and three very different brothers are born
723.howItsDone: Vidura's counsel to the king, the Vidura Niti in the Udyoga Parva, is read by some Hindus as a short guide to wise and honest living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambika shut her eyes, and Dhritarashtra was born blind. A widow too frightened to look.

Same palace, same sage, a different widow. Satyavati sends Vyasa to the younger princess, Ambalika. When she sees him, the blood leaves her face. She doesn't shut her eyes, as her sister did; her fear shows on her face instead. And the Kuru house is about to get three brothers: the blind one, the pale one, and one nobody planned for at all.
screen: `A DIFFERENT WIDOW.` → `SHE GOES PALE.` → `ONE NOBODY PLANNED FOR.`

segments.voice: Vyasa tells his mother: because she turned pale, the son will be pale, and that will be his name. Pandu, the pale one. He'll be a mighty prince, Vyasa says, and his own sons will be great. Two heirs now, one blind and one pale. Satyavati, still not at peace, asks for one more son from the elder widow. But Ambika can't face him again. She remembers his face and his smell, and does something no one expected: she dresses her maid in her own ornaments and sends her in her place. The maid isn't afraid. She rises when he enters, greets him with respect, and serves him. Vyasa is pleased. You are no longer a servant, he tells her, and your son will be virtuous and wise. He tells his mother everything, how the princess deceived him and how the maid honored him, and goes back to the forest. That son is Vidura. The text later says he is the god of dharma himself, born as a man because of a sage's curse; that's a story for another day. So here are the three brothers. One can't see. One is pale. And the son of a servant, born of a woman who simply showed respect, will grow up to be the palace's voice of wisdom, and, because of his mother's place, the one who can never be king. This is the generation before the cousins. Their sons will meet on the field.
screen: `PANDU, THE PALE ONE.` · `A MAID IN THE PRINCESS'S JEWELS.` · `SHE GREETS HIM WITH RESPECT.` · `VIDURA, THE WISE ONE.`

Pandu, the pale one, born because his mother's face went white with fear, now one of three brothers: the blind, the pale, and the wise.

724.title: the birth of the cousins
724.hook: the three brothers grow up, the pale one is crowned, and a princess of Gandhara learns her husband is blind and ties a cloth over her own eyes
724.carry: a strip of cloth, folded and tied
724.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings Gandhari is remembered as a figure of pativrata, devotion to a husband, and the blindfold is the image tellers and painters use for her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandu the pale, and Vidura, the maid's son. She simply showed him respect.

A strip of cloth, folded over and over, tied behind the head. A young princess named Gandhari, from the land of Gandhara, has been promised to a prince of the Kurus. Then she learns that he is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it, and binds her own eyes. Before we get to why, see the boys grow up.
screen: `A CLOTH, FOLDED MANY TIMES.` → `A PROMISED PRINCESS.` → `SHE BINDS HER OWN EYES.`

segments.voice: With the three boys born, the text says, the land of the Kurus flourishes: rains on time, full harvests, cities busy and safe. Bhishma raises the princes as his own. Dhritarashtra, the text says, becomes the strongest; Pandu, the finest archer; and Vidura has no equal in knowing dharma. Then, who rules? Dhritarashtra is the eldest, but the text says his blindness passes him over. Vidura is wise, but his mother was a servant, so he's passed over too. The crown goes to Pandu, the younger. Some readers find, in a firstborn watching his younger brother take the throne, a seed of much that follows. Now Bhishma looks for wives. He hears of Gandhari, daughter of the king of Gandhara, and asks for her for Dhritarashtra. Her family hesitates over a blind groom, then agrees. When Gandhari hears, she binds her eyes, resolving, the text says, out of regard for her husband, never to have more than he has. Her brother, Shakuni, brings her to Hastinapura. Remember his name. Readers take the blindfold more than one way. Some see a wife's complete devotion. Some see a woman refusing to be the one who sees, in a marriage she didn't choose. Some see grief worn on the face. The text gives the reason in her husband's honor and leaves the rest of her silent. Now two people who cannot see sit beside the throne, one by birth and one by choice, and a pale king sits on it.
screen: `THE KURU LAND FLOURISHES.` · `THE CROWN GOES TO PANDU.` · `GANDHARI BINDS HER EYES.` · `SHAKUNI BRINGS HER HOME.`

Gandhari, the princess who bound her own eyes, out of regard for the blind husband she married, Dhritarashtra.

725.title: the birth of the cousins
725.hook: King Pandu, out hunting, shoots a deer that turns out to be a sage, and the dying sage's curse shuts the door on his sons
725.carry: you've killed me in a moment of love
725.howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is an important value in Hindu traditions, and stories like Kindama's are retold to show how seriously a harm, even in a lawful hunt, can be taken.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown went to Pandu, and Gandhari bound her eyes. A strip of cloth, folded and tied.

A stag and a doe, together in a quiet forest clearing. A king on the hunt sees them through the trees, draws his bow, and shoots, quickly, without warning. The arrows strike the stag, and it falls. Then, lying in the grass, it speaks in a man's voice. King Pandu has just shot a sage.
screen: `A STAG AND A DOE.` → `THE ARROWS STRIKE.` → `THE DEER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Back up a little. Pandu has had a good reign. At her self-choice, the princess Kunti, adopted daughter of King Kuntibhoja, chose Pandu for her husband. Bhishma also brought him a second wife, Madri, sister of the king of the Madras. Pandu won wars and filled the treasury. Then he went to live in the forest with both wives, and spent his days hunting. That's where he meets the deer. The stag is a sage named Kindama, who had taken a deer's form to be with his wife. As he dies, he says: even a king who hunts should not strike creatures in a moment like this. You've killed me in a moment of love. So hear this: when you go to your wife in love, you will die. And he dies. Pandu is undone. He grieves for the sage, and for himself: a king with no son, who now can never father one. So he gives up the royal life entirely, to live as an ascetic, begging, fasting, with no home. He gives his jewels and royal robes to Brahmanas, and sends his attendants back to Hastinapura with the news. Kunti and Madri refuse to go back; they'll practice austerities beside him. Notice the turn. Yesterday the crown passed over the blind brother. Today the crowned king sits in a forest, unable to have heirs, while Dhritarashtra and Gandhari remain in the palace. The story has quietly tipped, and Pandu begins to ask how the line can go on without him.
screen: `KUNTI AND MADRI.` · `A KING GOES TO THE FOREST.` · `KINDAMA'S CURSE.` · `A KING WITH NO HEIRS.`

segments.voice: Pandu's arrow left the bow in an instant, and the curse lasted the rest of his life. Bring to mind one quick action of yours that had long consequences, good or hard, and without judging it, trace it the way you'd follow a river from its source. Then rest in the breath alone.
Shapa, a curse: the sage Kindama's dying words to the king whose arrow struck him in a moment of love.

726.title: the birth of the cousins
726.hook: in the forest, Kunti tells Pandu about a mantra a sage gave her as a girl, and three gods are called
726.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Indra is praised in Vedic hymns, Vayu is the wind and the breath, and Dharma is righteousness itself; in this story they become fathers of the Pandava brothers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandu's arrow, Kindama's curse, and a king in the forest with no way to have sons. You've killed me in a moment of love.

Years before any of this, a girl named Kunti served a sage in her father's house. He was Durvasa, hard to please, and she served him so carefully that, when he left, he gave her a gift: a mantra. With it she could call any god she chose, and have a son by him. She has kept it quiet ever since. Now her husband sits in the forest, cursed, asking how his line can go on.
screen: `A GIRL SERVES A SAGE.` → `A MANTRA, GIVEN.` → `KEPT QUIET FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: Pandu raises it first. He tells Kunti of the old custom, the same one that brought him into the world through Vyasa, and asks her to have sons for him by a worthy man. Kunti answers with her secret: the mantra. Pandu is overjoyed. Which god first? He chooses Dharma, the god of righteousness, so the eldest son will be just. Kunti calls, Dharma comes, and a son is born. A voice from the sky blesses the child, the text says, and he's named Yudhishthira. Next Pandu asks for a son of great strength. Kunti calls Vayu, the wind, and Bhima is born. The text shows what he is: as an infant he tumbles from his mother's lap onto a mountain, and it's the rock that shatters. Then Pandu wants a son foremost among warriors. He keeps vows himself, and Kunti calls Indra, king of the gods. Arjuna is born, and again a voice from the sky speaks over him. Three sons: justice, strength, and skill. But notice what Kunti doesn't say. She tells Pandu about the mantra, not everything about how she first learned what it could do. That piece waits for days ahead. And notice the shape. A line with no heir, a hidden gift from a sage, and a woman who finally speaks about it. Satyavati's secret saved the Kuru house once. Now Kunti's does the same, a generation on.

727.title: the birth of the cousins
727.hook: the cousins grow up under one roof, and a rivalry is born with them
727.howItsDone: Some Hindu families tell the Mahabharata to children a piece at a time, and the boyhood of Bhima and Duryodhana, with the poisoned meal and the serpent realm, is one of the pieces told.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti's mantra called Dharma, Vayu and Indra, and three sons were born. Justice, strength, and skill.

A fruit tree in a royal garden, boys up in its branches reaching for fruit. Below stands Bhima, the second son of Pandu. He kicks the trunk, and the boys come tumbling down with the fruit. In the water he holds his cousins under until they gasp. In the dust he drags them by the hair. The Mahabharata says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play. But one of the boys on the ground is Duryodhana, the eldest son of Dhritarashtra. And he doesn't forget.
screen: `A TREE FULL OF COUSINS.` → `BHIMA KICKS THE TRUNK.` → `DURYODHANA DOESN'T FORGET.`

segments.voice: The story moves quickly now. Madri, with Kunti's help, has twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva. In Hastinapura, Gandhari's sons are born, Duryodhana the eldest. In the forest, Pandu dies. Sages bring Kunti and the five sons of Pandu to Hastinapura, and the two families of cousins live in one palace, studying, eating and playing together. Bhima is stronger than all of them, and never lets them forget it. Duryodhana watches, and the story says jealousy takes hold of him. So he arranges a day of water sports by the Ganga, with pavilions and food. Into Bhima's food goes poison. When Bhima, worn out and heavy, lies down by the river, Duryodhana binds him and pushes him into the water. Bhima sinks down into the realm of the Nagas, the serpent people. The snakes bite him, and in the story their venom works against the poison. The Naga king receives him, and Bhima is given a drink that makes him stronger still. Back in Hastinapura, the brothers come home without him. Kunti is frantic and says aloud what she suspects. Vidura tells her to keep quiet: if she accuses Duryodhana openly, he may turn on her other sons. Then Bhima walks home, alive and stronger, and tells his brothers everything. Yudhishthira's answer: say nothing for now, and guard one another. The cousins were born in one family. Now something else has been born between them.

728.title: Karna's abandonment
728.hook: a girl in a king's house is given a mantra by a sage, and tries it on the sun

728.howItsDone: Some Hindus greet the rising sun with folded hands or an offering of water, honoring Surya, the god Pritha called with Durvasa's mantra.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the birth of the cousins: rough play, a poisoned meal, and a grudge that started young.

Two days ago, Kunti told Pandu about a sage's mantra, and held one piece back. Today the poem steps back in time to tell it. Before Kunti was a queen, she was a girl called Pritha, raised in the house of a king named Kuntibhoja. When the sage Durvasa came as a guest, the hard work of looking after him fell to her, and she did it well. His gift was the mantra. Now she is young, unmarried, alone with words that can summon a god.
screen: `PRITHA, IN KUNTIBHOJA'S HOUSE.` → `DURVASA'S GIFT.` → `DO THE WORDS WORK?`

segments.voice: With the mantra, Durvasa told her, she could call any god she liked, and that god would come and give her a son. Then he left. And the text says that, out of curiosity, she tries it. She looks up at the rising sun and speaks the mantra. And Surya, the sun god, comes. Here the story slows down, because Pritha is frightened. She tells him she only wanted to see if the gift worked. She's a girl in her father's house; she asks him to go. Surya answers that a god called by this mantra can't return for nothing. A son will be born. But he promises her something too: she'll remain a maiden afterward, her honor kept. So, at the week's end, the story hands us a beginning older than all the others. Before the five brothers, before the cousins, Kunti had a son. Nobody in the palace knows it. Notice how human the scene is. There's no villain in it: a sage's gift, a girl's curiosity, a god who keeps the rules of the mantra, and fear. Out of that fear, over the next few days, will come a choice that echoes through the whole poem.
screen: `A SAGE'S GIFT: A MANTRA.` · `SHE TRIES IT ON THE SUN.` · `SURYA COMES, AND SHE IS AFRAID.` · `A SON BEFORE ALL THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `NOBODY IN THE PALACE KNOWS.`
